title: Lesson 5: Bridge Analyses

5.1 What Is a Bridge Variable?
Bridge variables are computational or behavioral summary statistics that bridge the state-space model to:

Trait-level predictors (Age, depression, memory self-report) — behavioral Stage 2
Neural activity — second-level fMRI regression (who has larger PE beta?)
Connectivity patterns — gPPI and DCM PEB covariates

The design principle: extract model-based quantities from behavior first, test their neural correlates independently. This prevents double dipping.

title: Lesson 3: Metacognitive Accuracy
text:
3.1 Two Levels of Sensitivity
Type-1 (object level): How well does recall discriminate remembered from forgotten items? Standard d’.
Type-2 (metacognitive level): How well does the participant’s confidence (JOL) discriminate their own correct from incorrect responses? Meta-d’.
From Maniscalco & Lau (2012): meta-d’ is “what d’ would need to be if the observer’s sensitivity were perfectly aligned with their confidence.”
\[M\text{-ratio} = \frac{\text{meta-}d'}{d'} \qquad \text{(metacognitive efficiency)}\]
M-ratio = 1.0 means perfect efficiency; < 1.0 means suboptimal access to the internal signal.

title: Lesson 1: The Internal Feedback Loop
text:
1.1 Why a Feedback Loop?
In most fMRI memory studies, parametric modulators are static stimulus properties. This pipeline takes a different approach: the regressors are outputs of a dynamical system that evolves over the experiment.
Participants form expectations. After ten face-scene pairs you have a sense of how well you’re learning. When a new pair surprises you — much easier or harder than expected — that surprise is a prediction error: the gap between what happened and what your internal model predicted.
This maps onto the delta-rule, adapted for metacognition where:

The state \(S_t^{(c)}\) is a running estimate of learning quality for category \(c\)
The observation is the JOL (1=Unlikely, 2=Maybe, 3=Likely)
There is no external feedback — the loop is entirely internal

title: Lesson 1: The Internal Feedback Loop
text:
1.2 The Model Equations
Transition equation: \[S_t^{(c)} = S_{t-1}^{(c)} + \alpha \cdot \underbrace{(JOL_{t-1} - S_{t-1}^{(c)})}_{\text{PE}_{t-1}}\]
Prediction error: \[PE_t = JOL_t - S_t^{(c)}\]
\(\alpha \in (0,1)\) is the learning rate. High \(\alpha\) = rapid adaptation; low \(\alpha\) = stable slow-moving expectation. States are tracked separately per category, one shared \(\alpha\) per participant.

1.4 The Critical Identity: JOL = State + PE
This is the most important algebraic fact in the entire pipeline. It holds by construction at every trial:
\[JOL_t \equiv S_t + PE_t\]

    ×
  
  
  

This isn’t a modeling choice — it is a mathematical inevitability. Understanding this identity is prerequisite for Lesson 4 on GLM design.

title: JOL Internal Feedback Pipeline: A Practical Course
text:
This is a five-lesson course built directly from the code in the JOL computation pipeline. Each lesson explains why the code is designed the way it is, shows you the actual implementation, and gives you runnable examples you can modify in your browser.
The pipeline answers one scientific question: How do people build and update internal beliefs about their own learning performance, without any external feedback?

title: JOL Internal Feedback Pipeline: A Practical Course
text:
The Big Picture
Participants study paired images (face-scene or face-object) and after each pair judge how likely they are to remember it later — a Judgment of Learning (JOL). There is no feedback. Then, in a later memory test, we see what they actually recalled.
The pipeline models this as a genuine feedback loop: internal states generate predictions, observations violate those predictions (creating errors), and those errors update the states. This loop is the computational engine of metacognition.
     JOL observation
          ↓
    Prediction Error  ←──── State at time t
     (JOL − State)               ↑
          ↓                      │
     Update Rule ────────────────┘
   S_t = S_{t-1} + α × PE_{t-1}
This loop-based view — inspired by Nicole Rust’s work on neural feedback — is what separates this analysis from a simple GLM of confidence ratings.

title: JOL Internal Feedback Pipeline: A Practical Course
text:
Key Equations Reference
State transition (delta rule): \[S_t^{(c)} = S_{t-1}^{(c)} + \alpha \cdot \underbrace{(JOL_{t-1} - S_{t-1}^{(c)})}_{\text{Prediction Error}_{t-1}}\]
Prediction error: \[PE_t = JOL_t - S_t\]
Critical identity (causes collinearity — Lesson 4): \[JOL_t = S_t + PE_t \quad \forall t\]
Metacognitive efficiency (Lesson 3): \[M\text{-ratio} = \frac{\text{meta-}d'}{d'}\]
